title: Can We Differentiate Between Self-Reported Skills and Traits? A Possible Refinement of the BESSI and Its Validity in Italian High School Students
authors: Pellegrino, Gerardo and Meneghetti, Chiara and Carretti, Barbara and Feraco, Tommaso
abstract: Recent research has emphasized the conceptual distinction between personality traits and social, emotional, and behavioral (SEB) skills. However, their self-report measures show substantial empirical overlap. This study introduces and evaluates the Behavioral, Emotional, and Social Skills Inventory—Dual Rating (BESSI-Dual Rating), a modified version of the original BESSI designed to reduce this overlap. A sample of 598 Italian high school students completed the BESSI-Dual Rating, a Big Five personality inventory, and measures of academic and socio-emotional outcomes. Confirmatory factor analyses supported the structural validity of the BESSI-Dual Rating. Compared to previous BESSI validation studies, BESSI-Dual Rating scores showed improved discriminant and incremental validity relative to the corresponding traits. Furthermore, students perceived skill- and tendency-based items as meaningfully distinct—contrary to findings from prior research using alternative instruments. Parent-reported SEB skills provided additional support for the validity of the skill measures. These findings suggest that minor but targeted refinements in questionnaire design can enhance the empirical differentiation between skills and traits. © The Author(s) 2026

title: Self-Assessment of Social-Emotional Skills in Primary Students: Psychometric Evaluation of the Digital Screening Instrument GraSEF
authors: Kogler, Andrea and Barth, Maximilian and Prinz, Katharina and Paleczek, Lisa and Gasteiger-Klicpera, Barbara
abstract: Early assessment of social-emotional skills is crucial for identifying children at risk and implementing targeted interventions. To address the scarcity of reliable self-reports for young children, we developed the GraSEF, a digital screening instrument for primary students. GraSEF utilizes a situational judgment format to assess internalizing/externalizing behavior, social withdrawal, problem-solving, alongside self-reports for prosocial behavior and emotion regulation strategies. This study examines the instrument’s psychometric properties in a sample of 474 s-graders in Austria (M<sub>age</sub> = 7.66 years, SD = 0.42; 52.1% girls). Divergent and convergent validity were examined via teacher- and self-report scales. Confirmatory factor analyses supported a robust six-factor model with scalar invariance across gender and family language. Results demonstrated acceptable to good internal consistency, and stable test-retest reliability. However, low student-teacher agreement was observed, which warrant further investigation. GraSEF proves to be a reliable instrument for assessing student’s social-emotional skills and behavior problems. © The Author(s) 2026.

title: A Practical Approach to Trauma: Empowering Interventions, 2ND EDITION
journal: A Practical Approach to Trauma: Empowering Interventions, 2ND EDITION
authors: Dass-Brailsford, Priscilla
abstract: This book is invaluable for clinicians who provide trauma-focused care. Adopting a practitioner’s perspective, the book focuses on practical applications and skill-building. Updated with DSM-5-TR content throughout, the book begins with an overview of the trauma field and historical and intergenerational trauma, and proceeds to review individual, group, and community interventions using cognitive-behavioral, relational, affect regulation, mindfulness, and psychopharmacologic approaches. Besides models of trauma therapy, other topics include the neurobiology of trauma, racial trauma, political trauma, community and school crises, and pandemics and natural disasters. Current theoretical perspectives and methods that provide a paradigm for stage appropriate, culture-based therapy, which can be integrated into existing therapeutic orientations, are outlined. Coverage of a wide range of trauma and inclusion of evidence-based interventions and current theoretical and research literature makes it comprehensive. An ecological perspective helps readers focus on the importance of viewing behavior in the context of social settings and the physical and psychosocial barriers to trauma recovery. The book’s empowering approach shifts attention from deficits and dependence toward resources and resiliency. Both empowerment and ecological theory integrate a critical understanding of the cultural and sociopolitical environment that contributes to trauma, thus restoring clients’ personal control and recovery. The book provides specific information on working with rape survivors, conducting groups for battered women, facilitating community meetings and debriefings, and developing crisis protocols for schools or communities. Client vignettes gleaned from clinical experience provide a hands-on resource for clinicians and graduate students training to become mental health providers. © Oxford University Press 2026.

title: Hypotheses and Concepts Advantages and Limitations of a Systemic and Ecological Assessment of Executive Functions in Children and Adolescents
authors: Weisse, Mélissa and Dardier, Virginie and Scotto Di Vettimo, Solenne and Tsimba, Véronique and Troles, Nolwenn and Douguet, Anne-Sophie and Jouan, Virginia and Lacroix, Agnès
abstract: Executive functions (EFs) are high-level functions of human cognition and have been studied since the early 20th century. The evolution of theoretical models of EFs highlights the importance of taking into account all systemic influences, whether biological, environmental, or individual, when assessing these functions, particularly in children. This indicates the necessity to propose an integrative perspective for evaluating EFs. To do so, we drew on Bronfenbrenner’s ecosystemic model to underline the importance of an ecological assessment. This article reviews the arguments in favor of the ecological assessment of EFs and acknowledged their limitations. The arguments came from (a) the biological level—recognizing that cerebral architecture, particularly the prefrontal cortex, which underlies EFs and its development with age encourages us to reconsider inter-individual differences, and (b) the environmental level—considering the influence of the family, educational, or even cultural system enables us to contextualize and take a step back from performance. The relationship between cold and hot executive functions was also considered. The development of ecological assessment tools, closer to the strategies and processes spontaneously implemented in everyday life, may lead to a more appropriate assessment of executive functioning, and thus to increasingly tailored support. © 2026 The Author(s). Published by IMR Press.

title: PSYCHOLOGY IN EDUCATION: INDIVIDUAL DIFFERENCES AND LEARNING
journal: Psychology in Education: Individual Differences and Learning
authors: Symes, Wendy and Putwain, David W. and Nicholson, Laura J. and Lichtenfeld, Stephanie and Schmidt, Fabian T. C. and Skipper, Yvonne
abstract: This essential textbook provides a comprehensive overview of the psychological factors that influence student learning and achievement. It addresses the fundamental questions of why and how some students outperform others by examining research and theory on key constructs. These include intelligence, personality, motivation and emotions, with a focus on their definitions, measurement and crucial roles in education. Key Features: • Defines key psychological factors that play an important role in student achievement • Evaluates how these psychological factors influence student learning • Investigates factors that can influence the development of these psychological factors, including genetics and experience • Demonstrates how enhancing students’ thoughts and feelings can influence their academic performance • Presents clear summaries of key points and stimulating questions to encourage understanding, as well as supplementary material to support further study Psychology in Education is highly relevant to students of educational psychology with an interest in individual differences in educational contexts. It is particularly relevant for students studying individual differences modules on Psychology of Education programmes. It is also a useful resource for teachers and educational practitioners seeking to understand the psychological dynamics at play in the classroom, enabling them to design lessons that engage and motivate students. © Wendy Symes, David W. title: HumanCorps: Redesigning Organisations for the Wisdom Age
journal: HumanCorps: Redesigning Organisations for the Wisdom Age
authors: Lopianowski, Andrew and Pino, Mike
abstract: HumanCorps delivers a practical blueprint for leaders to transform their organisations from outdated Industrial-Age models into adaptive, human-centered enterprises that thrive in the AI-powered Wisdom Age. Thought-provoking and timely, the book offers a comprehensive framework that combines compelling case studies, expert interviews, and actionable strategies for organisational transformation. It provides detailed implementation guidance, diagnostic tools, and step-by-step approaches to building resilient businesses that prioritise human potential while leveraging technology. Each chapter includes visual models, executive action checklists, and structured summaries that translate complex concepts into immediately applicable solutions for real-world challenges. Ideal for forward-thinking executives, senior managers, and transformation leaders, this book is tailored for decision-makers in private and public sectors who are navigating systemic upheaval. Whether you’re a CEO, HR director, or strategy leader, you need these insights and tools to guide your organisation into a thriving future. © 2027 Andrew Lopianowski and Mike Pino.

title: DIGITAL IDENTITIES, AI ETHICS, AND MENTAL HEALTH: Impacts of Technology on Cyber Behaviors and Personality Traits
journal: Digital Identities, Ai Ethics, and Mental Health: Impacts of Technology on Cyber Behaviors and Personality Traits
authors: Elsayary, Areej
abstract: This highly topical book provides an integrated framework for understanding how artificial intelligence, personality traits, gender, and cultural contexts shape youth digital engagement and mental health outcomes. Grounded in cyberpsychology and extensive empirical research, AI ethics, and developmental psychology, this book addresses the urgent need for evidence-based approaches to supporting young people's well-being in an increasingly AI-mediated digital world. It explores the dual nature of digital technology, offering unique opportunities for connection, learning, and self-expression while simultaneously introducing distinctive risks to mental health and well-being. It examines how personality trait models mediate the effects of cyber behavior on well-being and ethical AI engagement. Further topics include an exploration of AI as an active participant in shaping youth behavior and identity, how personality traits significantly predict resilience to online risks and ethical AI engagement, gender differences in digital engagement creating distinct opportunities and vulnerabilities, cultural contexts fundamentally shaping cyber behaviors and ethical perspectives, and that ethical AI design must prioritize youth developmental vulnerabilities. With actionable recommendations to foster digital well-being and responsible AI use, this book is a comprehensive guide for promoting ethical and psychologically healthy digital practices. The unique blend of theoretical insights, empirical data, and practical interventions makes this book an essential resource for students and academics in cyberpsychology, social psychology and identity, AI ethics, cyber behavior studies, and mental health. It will also be of interest to mental health professionals, researchers, policymakers, and educators interested in understanding the impact of cyber behaviors on youth well-being. © 2027 Areej ElSayary. title: Health Psychology: An Interdisciplinary Approach
authors: Ragin, Deborah Fish
abstract: Now in its fourth edition, Health Psychology takes a truly interdisciplinary approach to studying health psychology, and offers a comprehensive overview of the subareas within this fascinating subject. Fully revised to reflect current research and studies, and now in full color, the book includes new content on the impact of COVID-19 and greater coverage of health diversity. It unpacks the issue of social inequities in health by addressing how race and social economies have been traditionally confounded. The author achieves this by focusing on five systems that affect individual health outcomes: individual, family/community, social/physical environment, health care systems, and health policy. The social ecological perspective on health psychology creates a depth of understanding of the diverse facets of health, and examines health from a global perspective by exploring the impact of infectious and chronic illnesses both regionally and globally. This new edition has been packed with updated statistics and references, as well as helpful video links infused throughout, to actively engage readers in each topic. While grounded in psychology, the book incorporates perspectives from anthropology, biology, economics, environmental studies, medicine, public health, and sociology, and will be of particular interest to undergraduate students in health psychology and public health and for masters’ students of health psychology. For additional instructor resources, please visit www.routledge.com/9781032292557, which includes lecture slides, an instructor manual, and test bank. © 2025 Deborah Fish Ragin.

title: 20 years of firm growth literature in the international small business journal: Taking stock, looking ahead
journal: International Small Business Journal: Researching Entrepreneurship
authors: Marconatto, Diego Antonio Bittencourt and Levie, Jonathan
abstract: Over the past two decades, the International Small Business Journal (ISBJ) has played a pivotal role in shaping scholarly understanding of small and medium-sized enterprise (SME) growth. This commentary presents a systematic literature review of 92 ISBJ articles published between 2004 and 2023, examining geographic coverage, theoretical foundations, methodological approaches, growth measures, and thematic trends. Our analysis reveals areas of consolidation and knowledge gaps, including limited attention on the regions beyond Western advanced economies, family and mid-sized firms, the entrepreneur’s role, AI and digitalization, the contingent nature of growth, new theoretical perspectives, weak integration of institutional contexts, and the dominance of outcome-centric views of growth. Moving beyond gaps internal to articles in the ISBJ, we consider these patterns in light of the broader entrepreneurship and management literature and outline research avenues accordingly. In doing so, we aim to reinforce the ISBJ’s role in advancing a more integrative and future-oriented agenda for SME growth research. © The Author(s) 2026

title: HEALTH PROMOTION AND AGING: Practical Applications for Health Professionals, Ninth Edition
journal: Health Promotion and Aging: Practical Applications for Health Professionals, Ninth Edition
authors: Albert, Steven M.
abstract: This book promotes healthy aging by demonstrating how health practitioners, program developers, and policymakers can prevent or manage disease and make large-scale improvements toward health and wellness in the older adult population. This ninth edition encompasses new research that substantially updates previous recommendations. It provides important new content on aging (the potential for geroscience to change how we age), health (e.g., new therapies to control obesity and cognitive decline), and the aging services infrastructure (how health is actually delivered to older people). The book includes key terms and learning objectives at the start of each chapter; questions to ponder within each chapter; boxes throughout containing information to reflect upon, and new chapter-ending summaries. These summaries do not just list highlights in each chapter, but synthesize an overarching theme or themes of each chapter. The book is practical, including health-promoting tools, resource lists, assessment tools, illustrations, checklists, and tables. © 2026 Springer Publishing Company, LLC.

title: Behavioral tendencies of success: toward a verb-like conception of successful life functioning
authors: Irvin, Roberta L. and Vohra, Pranika and Lawrence, Grace A. and Robinson, Michael D.
abstract: Can a test reveal whether individuals will succeed or struggle in their lives? This question was pursued through the use of a Behavioral Tendencies in Life Test (BTLT), which asks individuals whether they would respond to 40 life-modeling scenarios in each of 4 ways. A prototype of the successful person was created using the same materials and then applied to each person’s BTLT ratings. In two studies (total N = 352), participants who received higher, relative to lower, behavioral tendencies of success (BT-S) scores used approach-related coping strategies, pursued important goals, were capable of meeting their basic psychological needs, and reported higher levels of life satisfaction and flourishing. Individuals who received lower BT-S scores were prone to internalizing and externalizing problems and were deemed to be less skilled by peers. The research integrates bottom-up and top-down perspectives in emphasizing the verb-like nature of successful (versus unsuccessful) life functioning. © 2026 Informa UK Limited, trading as Taylor & Francis Group.

title: Cultural variations in the relationship between school belonging and social-emotional skills: a multi-group structural equation modeling (SEM) analysis
authors: Tan, Yuting and Mendoza, Norman B. and Yeung, Susanna Siu-sze
abstract: Social-emotional skills are crucial for student development yet they decline significantly during secondary education globally, raising questions about effective interventions. While school belonging is theorized to support social-emotional development, its cross-cultural universality remains contested. This study examined associations between school belonging and ten social-emotional skill dimensions across eight cultural regions using PISA 2022 data from 527,255 students in 74 countries. Multi-group structural equation modeling revealed positive associations globally, but substantial cross-cultural variation emerged. Harmony-embeddedness cultures (Latin America, South/Southeast Asia) showed the strongest effects, while autonomy-oriented cultures (Western Europe, English-speaking) and Confucian societies exhibited minimal associations. These findings challenge universal assumptions about belonging interventions, demonstrating that cultural values function as crucial contextual factors that amplify, suppress, or redirect belonging’s developmental impact. Results necessitate culturally responsive approaches to social-emotional development rather than one-size-fits-all interventions, highlighting the importance of understanding diverse pathways to human flourishing across cultural contexts. © The Author(s) 2026.

title: Happiness in the Marketplace: A Study of Consumption, Consumers and Wellbeing
authors: Lee, Dong-Jin and Joseph Sirgy, M.
abstract: This book provides a systematic review and analysis of the literature on product-related, situational, organizational, and cultural factors influencing people’s happiness in the marketplace. The authors, senior experts in the field, make specific recommendations to design and implement consumer wellbeing strategies. These recommendations are for marketing executives to maximize their effectiveness and help consumers achieve optimal levels of happiness (overall happiness, consumer happiness, and consumption happiness), which in turn could enhance organizational return on investment through customer loyalty, repeat patronage, sales, and profit. The book reviews and integrates learnings from the research on happiness in several fields of study, namely, quality-of-life studies, marketing, consumer studies, social psychology, and behavioral economics, and is of interest to marketing executives and academics from various fields working on consumers and consumer wellbeing. © The Editor(s) (if applicable) and The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2025.

title: Social, emotional, and behavioral skills as resources for student engagement: A one-year longitudinal study in high school students
authors: Pellegrino, Gerardo and Feraco, Tommaso and Meneghetti, Chiara and Carretti, Barbara
abstract: Social, emotional, and behavioral (SEB) skills refer to capacities that support social relationships, emotion regulation, and engagement with new experiences. These skills are considered crucial for high school students' academic success and well-being. The present study examined the longitudinal associations between five SEB skill domains (self-management, social engagement, cooperation, innovation, and emotional resilience) and four dimensions of student engagement (affective, behavioral, cognitive, and agentic). A sample of 1555 Italian high school students completed self-report measures of SEB skills and engagement at the beginning (T1), middle (T2), and end (T3) of the academic year. Latent change score modelling showed that student engagement generally declined across the school year, particularly between T1 and T2. However, students with higher levels of self-management, innovation, and social engagement at T1 showed smaller declines in engagement. Overall, these findings suggest that SEB skills help students sustain engagement, especially during the first part of the school year. Educational relevance statement: Social, emotional, and behavioral (SEB) skills are increasingly recognized as key competencies that foster student engagement in learning and academic activities. Using a comprehensive SEB framework and a three-wave longitudinal design, our study examined whether SEB skills contribute to the maintenance of engagement across the school year. Results indicated that students who reported higher levels of self-management, innovation, and social engagement also experienced smaller decreases in engagement, although the effects varied across engagement dimensions. Overall, these findings highlight the educational value of integrating SEB skills instruction into school curricula. Strengthening these skills may help students sustain engagement throughout the academic year, with potential benefits for academic achievement and well-being. © 2026 The Authors

title: Expanding the Limits of Individual and Family Therapies: A Critical Realist Approach
journal: Palgrave Texts in Counselling and Psychotherapy
authors: Pocock, David
abstract: This book invites individual therapists to think systemically (including issues of social justice) and family therapists to explore a deeper understanding of the individual in contexts, including the domain of the unconscious. Using a critical realist framework, it promotes multiple perspectives—often novel combinations from dissimilar psychotherapy traditions—to expand holistic understanding and provide a richer variety of resources to bring to co-constructed therapeutic encounters. It uses a critical examination of the often-unspoken philosophical underpinnings of psychotherapy practices to re-vision a range of theory and practice considerations—theory choice, the role of science, knowing and not-knowing, emotion in the system, power and autonomy, collaboration and change, and sameness and otherness. All the preceding elements of the book are then brought together in the clinical topics of triangulation, aggressive out-of-control behaviour, and self-harm. Numerous brief case vignettes and longer case examples ensure that theory is always grounded in practice. © The Editor(s) (if applicable) and The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2024.

title: Vertical Sensemaking in Organisations: How Hierarchical Position Shapes Strategic Cognition
journal: Organizational Psychology, Leadership, and Sustainable Performance
authors: Roos, Göran and Bjartveit, Steinar
abstract: This chapter examines how hierarchical position shapes cognition and sensemaking in organisations. Drawing on sensemaking theory, the attention-based view, stratified systems theory, and the psychology of power, the authors develop a framework demonstrating how interpretation varies across executive, middle management, and operational levels. Eight mechanisms are identified: differential information access, scope of responsibility, temporal orientation, identity, social reference groups, risk perception, information distortion, and divergent mental models. Implications for strategic alignment, implementation failure, and decision quality are examined, followed by intervention principles across structural, process, communication, and cultural domains. Boundary conditions addressing organisational context, individual differences, and cross-cultural factors are specified. The chapter contributes theoretical advancement and practical guidance for diagnosing vertical sensemaking challenges and designing effective interventions. title: Influence of invalidating childhood environment and emotion regulation on academic procrastination; [Influência do ambiente invalidante infantil e regulação emocional na procrastinação acadêmica]; [Influencia del ambiente invalidante infantil y regulación emocional en la procrastinación académica...
authors: Indaver, María Herlein and Iriarte, Lucia and Furlan, Luis Alberto and Sánchez-Rosas, Javier
abstract: A debilitating childhood environment can lead to difficulties in emotional regulation, which contribute to academic procrastination. However, the direct effect of this environment on procrastination has been less studied. To explore this issue, 236 students from different Argentine universities were surveyed using self-selection sampling. Structural equation modeling was applied to analyze the relationships between variables. The results showed that emotional regulation significantly predicted procrastination, while the invalidating childhood environment did not have a direct effect, but rather an indirect effect mediated by emotional difficulties. These findings highlight the need to strengthen emotional regulation and foster validated parental environments to prevent procrastination in the university setting. © (2026), (Pontificia Universidad Catolica del Peru). title: Academic Lifestyle Medicine: A Curriculum for Medical Educators
journal: Academic Lifestyle Medicine: A Curriculum for Medical Educators
authors: Rippe, James M. and Frates, Beth
abstract: There is no longer any serious doubt that what individuals do in their daily lives profoundly impacts their short- and long-term health, quality of life, and risk of developing chronic diseases. Despite overwhelming evidence in this area, physicians often feel inadequately prepared to discuss these issues with their patients. This results from the relative lack of education for physicians in these components of lifestyle medicine. Authored by renowned cardiologist and lifestyle medicine researcher Dr. James Rippe and lifestyle medicine education and behavioral medicine expert Dr. Beth Frates, Academic Lifestyle Medicine: A Curriculum for Medical Educators blends state-of-the-art information on the robust medical literature supporting lifestyle medicine with an innovative approach to medical education. This book starts with an extensive discussion of the robust evidence that underlies the major components of lifestyle medicine including physical activity, nutrition, weight management, substance abuse and addiction, sleep, and positive connections to others. This information is then linked to how this evidence can be used to lower the risk of chronic diseases such as heart disease, diabetes, cancer, metabolic syndrome, brain health, cognitive function, and many other health issues. The authors then provide a specific framework for applying the principles of lifestyle medicine to all stages of medical education-from undergraduate to graduate training and continuing medical education. Additional specialty topics include the evidence supporting lifestyle medicine practice to ensure healthy aging, the unique lifestyle challenges for women and how lifestyle medicine applies to healthy habits amongst children and families. Other topics include how lifestyle medicine components interact with planetary health, health equity, and advocacy across numerous professional and regulatory groups. A volume in the Lifestyle Medicine Series, this book is a must-read for physicians wishing to understand the robust academic foundations of modern lifestyle medicine practice. It also provides an authoritative guide for physicians who are tasked with preparing the next generation of physicians in lifestyle medicine. © 2027 Taylor & Francis Group, LLC.

title: Large language models and social-emotional learning: Promise, limits, and conditions for responsible use
authors: Tang, Xin and Fang, Yirou and Wu, Tao and Pan, Xianglin and Zhan, Jian and Liu, Zepeng and Ali, Farhan and Guo, Jiesi and Chen, Jingyuan and Wu, Fei
abstract: The educational artificial intelligence literature has developed rapidly around cognitive uses of large language models (LLMs), with comparatively little systematic attention to their role in social-emotional learning (SEL). In this paper, we synthesize two strands of recent research to argue that contemporary LLMs warrant serious consideration as infrastructure for SEL. The first strand documents that contemporary LLMs can generate responses on social-emotional tasks that approach or exceed average human performance. The second strand reports growing empirical evidence that LLM-based interventions can support social-emotional skills development. We also provide further evidence with our own cross-linguistic evaluation of five LLMs (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, DeepSeek-R1, Ernie, and Qwen) using the OECD Survey of Social and Emotional Skills framework. Our results suggest that current models can display broad SEL-relevant response patterns, especially in English, and that these patterns are highly responsive to simple prompting. We close by outlining application scenarios and safeguards for responsible deployment, including privacy protection, cultural validation, transparent AI labelling, crisis escalation, and human oversight. © 2026

title: Social and emotional skills for nurturing parenting: A qualitative examination
authors: Beccassino, Luciana and Borbon, Juliana and Cuartas, Jorge and Rey-Guerra, Catalina and Gutierrez-Torres, Maria Alejandra and Guerra, Melissa and Baker-Henningham, Helen
abstract: Social and emotional skills develop within cultural contexts and shape parenting behaviors, yet little work has examined the specific skills parents themselves consider important for parenting, or the factors they perceive as supporting these skills, in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Centering parents' own conceptualizations, this two-phase descriptive qualitative study with 54 parents living in Colombia combined an initial phase of focus groups and individual interviews with a second phase of targeted individual interviews, and used thematic analysis to explore the social and emotional skills parents identify as relevant to parenting and the risk and protective factors perceived to hinder or enhance their development. Our findings highlight the importance of emotional awareness, self-regulation, communication, cooperation, and problem-solving skills in adulthood for nurturing parenting and promoting children's social and emotional development. Parents' upbringing and support networks emerged as significant factors shaping skill development and child-rearing practices. These findings emphasize the need for policies and interventions, grounded in caregivers' own perspectives, to promote social and emotional skills for parents in LMIC contexts.

title: Development and psychometric validation of the soft skills scale for primary school students
authors: Aygun, Hanife Esen and Asikcan, Mehmet and Zeren, Serife Gonca
abstract: This study aimed to develop a Soft Skills Scale for primary school students and to determine its psychometric properties. A total of 2,418 primary school students participated in the scale development process. Principal component analysis revealed a six-factor, 19-item structure explaining 41.37\% of the total variance. Confirmatory factor analysis provided additional evidence supporting the proposed six-factor structure, with acceptable model fit indices. Criterion-related validity was supported by a moderate positive correlation. Test-retest reliability, assessed over a four-week period, yielded a correlation coefficient of 0.83, indicating strong temporal stability. Internal consistency coefficients are Cronbach's alpha of 0.79 and McDonald's omega of 0.80 for the overall scale. The findings provide evidence supporting the reliability and construct validity of the SSS-S for assessing soft skills among primary school students within the context of the current sample. The Soft Skills Scale for primary school students address a significant gap in literature by providing one of the first scale designed to comprehensively assess interpersonal, cognitive, emotional, and behavioral components of soft skills in primary school students. The developed scale is expected to contribute to classroom-based interventions and school counseling practices. Additionally, the SSS-S has the potential to contribute to future international comparative studies. However, additional evidence regarding cross-cultural validity and measurement invariance is needed before such applications can be supported.

title: Self-Efficacy Predicts Differential Neuroticism Change in a Smartphone-Based Intervention
journal: JOURNAL OF PERSONALITY AND SOCIAL PSYCHOLOGY
authors: Kramer, Michael D. and Wright, Amanda J. and Haehner, Peter and Zimmermann, Johannes and Fluckiger, Christoph and Hopwood, Christopher J. and Bleidorn, Wiebke
abstract: Self-guided, digital interventions can help people change their personality traits in desired directions, including becoming less neurotic. However, little is known about how and why people differ in intervention-related changes. Theoretical models state that intentional personality change must be perceived as feasible and that being motivated to change is not sufficient to elicit lasting trait changes. Using a German-speaking sample (N = 446; M-age = 25.88; 85\% female; Residence: 47\% Switzerland, 26\% Germany, 26\% Austria, 1\% other), we tested whether self-efficacy and growth mindset predict change in multiple neuroticism measures across a 6-week intervention and 2-month follow-up. To isolate temporal processes during the intervention, we examined codevelopment of weekly neuroticism and self-efficacy and their week-to-week temporal associations. We found evidence for self-efficacy predicting differential neuroticism change but not for growth mindset. Participants with higher self-efficacy showed greater pre-post decreases in self-reported neuroticism and greater pre-post increases in emotional resilience than those with lower self-efficacy. At follow-up, participants with higher self-efficacy continued to improve more in neuroticism and emotional resilience. Last, higher self-efficacy in 1 week predicted lower neuroticism in the following week, and vice versa, independent of participants' overall trajectories. In contrast, there was no consistent evidence for between-person codevelopment of weekly self-efficacy and neuroticism across the intervention. Findings support theoretical expectations that perceived feasibility is a precondition for neuroticism change and suggest possible reinforcement mechanisms between weekly self-efficacy and neuroticism. We discuss implications for theory and future intervention studies.

title: Sense of purpose and perception of involution (Nei Juan): the role of actual-ideal self-discrepancy and future time perspective
authors: Yang, Guoliang and Wang, Zhihua and Fang, Miaoying and Wu, Weijiong and Wang, Ruiming
abstract: Objective The concurrent increase in ``hollowed-heart{''} syndrome (which describes a state of purposelessness) and involution anxiety severely impairs the psychological development of contemporary Chinese undergraduates. From a de-involution perspective, this study aimed to examine the relationship between sense of purpose and perceived involution, and to explore the mediating role of actual-ideal self-discrepancy and the moderating effect of future time perspective in this association. Method A total of 747 Chinese undergraduates completed online and offline questionnaires measuring the four core psychological variables. Results (1) Sense of purpose exerted a significant negative direct effect (beta = -0.27, p < 0.001) on perceived involution; (2) Actual-ideal self-discrepancy partially mediated this negative relationship (indirect effect = -0.06, SE = 0.01, 95\% CI {[}-0.08, -0.03]); (3) Future time perspective moderated the first-stage path of the indirect effect. Simple slope analyses showed that the sense of purpose-perceived involution association was significant at a low (M - 1SD) level of future time perspective (simple slope: beta = -0.24, p < 0.001), but was not significant at a high (M + 1SD) level of future time perspective (simple slope: beta = -0.02, p > 0.05), such that the mediating role of actual-ideal self-discrepancy was weaker among individuals with a higher future time perspective. Conclusion A stronger sense of purpose mitigates undergraduates' perceived involution by reducing actual-ideal self-discrepancy. Cultivating life purpose and future-oriented cognition may help alleviate undergraduates' involution anxiety. Based on self-discrepancy theory and socioemotional selectivity theory, these findings clarify the underlying mechanism of the involution perception and have practical implications for college mental health education and targeted stress interventions.
